solution_overview:
A sports club has 100 members. The numbers of members playing Soccer (S), Basketball (B), and Tennis (T) are represented by a Venn diagram. We assume each member has an equal probability of being selected, so probabilities are calculated as ratios of member counts to the total $N=100$. The key regions of the Venn diagram are defined as follows:

*   $N_S = 28$: members who play Soccer only.
*   $N_B = 20$: members who play Basketball only.
*   $N_T = 18$: members who play Tennis only.
*   $N_{SB} = 10$: members who play Soccer and Basketball, but not Tennis.
*   $N_{ST} = 7$: members who play Soccer and Tennis, but not Basketball.
*   $N_{BT} = 5$: members who play Basketball and Tennis, but not Soccer.
*   $N_{SBT} = 5$: members who play all three sports (Soccer, Basketball, and Tennis).

The total number of members playing at least one sport is the sum of these regions:
$$N_{S \cup B \cup T} = N_S + N_B + N_T + N_{SB} + N_{ST} + N_{BT} + N_{SBT}$$
$$N_{S \cup B \cup T} = 28 + 20 + 18 + 10 + 7 + 5 + 5$$
$$N_{S \cup B \cup T} = 93$$

The number of members playing none of the sports is the total membership minus those playing at least one sport:
$$N_{\text{none}} = N - N_{S \cup B \cup T}$$
$$N_{\text{none}} = 100 - 93 = 7$$

These counts will be used to calculate probabilities for various events.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The probability that a member plays at least one of the three sports corresponds to the union of the three sets, $P(S \cup B \cup T)$. This is the count of members playing at least one sport divided by the total number of members. From the setup, $N_{S \cup B \cup T} = 93$.

$$P(\text{at least one}) = \frac{N_{S \cup B \cup T}}{N}$$
$$P(\text{at least one}) = \frac{93}{100}$$
$$P(\text{at least one}) = 0.93 = 93\%$$

Since $93\% > 90\%$, the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The event that a member plays none of the three sports is the complement of the event that a member plays at least one of the three sports. For any event $A$, the probability of its complement $A^c$ is $P(A^c) = 1 - P(A)$.

Therefore, $P(\text{none}) = 1 - P(\text{at least one})$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The event that a member plays exactly one of the three sports means playing only Soccer, or only Basketball, or only Tennis. This corresponds to the sum of the counts $N_S$, $N_B$, and $N_T$.

$$P(\text{exactly one}) = \frac{N_S + N_B + N_T}{N}$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = \frac{28 + 20 + 18}{100}$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = \frac{66}{100}$$
$$P(\text{exactly one}) = 0.66 = 66\%$$

Since $66\% > 60\%$, the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The event that a member plays exactly two of the three sports, but not all three, means playing Soccer and Basketball (but not Tennis), or Soccer and Tennis (but not Basketball), or Basketball and Tennis (but not Soccer). This corresponds to the sum of the counts $N_{SB}$, $N_{ST}$, and $N_{BT}$.

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = \frac{N_{SB} + N_{ST} + N_{BT}}{N}$$
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = \frac{10 + 7 + 5}{100}$$
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = \frac{22}{100}$$
$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.22 = 22\%$$

The claim states this probability is less than $20\%$. We found $22\%$. Since $22\% \not< 20\%$, the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The probability that a member plays all three sports is the count $N_{SBT}$ divided by the total number of members.

$$P(\text{all three}) = \frac{N_{SBT}}{N}$$
$$P(\text{all three}) = \frac{5}{100}$$
$$P(\text{all three}) = 0.05$$

The probability that a member plays exactly two sports but not all three was calculated in the previous part:

$$P(\text{exactly two}) = 0.22$$

The claim compares $P(\text{all three})$ with one-fourth of $P(\text{exactly two})$:

$$\frac{1}{4} \times P(\text{exactly two}) = \frac{1}{4} \times 0.22$$
$$\frac{1}{4} \times 0.22 = 0.055$$

Comparing the two values:

$$0.05 < 0.055$$

Since $P(\text{all three})$ is indeed less than one-fourth of $P(\text{exactly two})$, the statement is True.
